paper.title: Income effects and labour supply: Evidence from a child benefits reform
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability statement (p. 18): 'The authors do not have permission to share data.' The analysis relies entirely on administrative data from Denmark supplied by Statistics Denmark, covering the entire Danish population. …

registers.years: 2008-2014 (children registered in BEF in each year from 2008-2014); births from 2000
registers.role: treatment construction, controls, linkage and sample frame
treatment construction and controls: monthly individual-level data on children and family composition, together with BEF
outcomes: monthly hours worked and monthly earnings reported by employers
validation of the constructed child benefit payments and exclusion of families with irregular payments
outcomes: annual individual and family income measures; also the income variables used for heterogeneity splits
treatment-group refinement: consultations with doctors regarding sterilisation procedures (model C sample restriction)
treatment-group refinement: consultations with doctors regarding sterilisation procedures
treatment-group refinement: consultations with doctors regarding sterilisation procedures

linkages: Personal identifiers of both parents and partners are observed, so family-level variables can be constructed, including an indicator equal to one if either partner in a couple has consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation
Children are linked to parents through the relevant parent ID in the population register BEF
Constructed child benefit payments (from BEF family composition) are validated against actual fourth-quarter payments in BOBO/BOTI
Monthly hours worked from BFL are aggregated across all jobs an individual holds in a month

sample.universe: Individuals in the Danish population registers who in January 2011 were married or in a cohabiting couple, had at least 2 children under 18 and no more than 4 children in total; analysed separately for women and men
sample.unit_of_observation: person-month (person-year for the income analyses in Tables 6 and 7)
selection_rules: Balanced panel with monthly observations of women and men covering September 2008 to December 2014 (observations before September 2008 excluded because a small change in child benefit amounts was implemented earlier in 2008)
Exclude people who are less than 25 years old by September 2008 or at least 60 years old by December 2014
Drop parents of children to whom child benefits are paid irregularly (e.g. children in foster care)
Exclude immigrants and children of immigrants (eligibility rules changed for immigrants in the sample period and elasticities may depend on cultural background)

For the main analysis, drop individuals who are self-employed at any point within the sample window, because hours worked are not observed for them (13.0%, 29,144 individuals, of men and 7.3%, 18,940 individuals, of women); the self-employed are included in the income analyses
In January 2011: at least 2 children under 18 (both registered in BEF in 2011, or 2012 for children born in 2011, with the relevant parent ID)
In January 2011: no more than 4 children in total
In January 2011: married or in a cohabiting couple
Balance the panel, excluding people not present in the Danish population registers and in the sample for the entire period September 2008 to December 2014

Model (C) only: limit to families in which at least one parent consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation prior to the announcement of the policy, and exclude families with young children (below the age of 3) throughout the sample period
Intensive-margin analysis only: unbalance the panel and delete all monthly observations with zero hours of work
sample.period: September 2008 to December 2014 (monthly); 2008 to 2014 (annual, for the income analyses)
sample.n_observations: 18,153,075 person-months for women and 14,655,450 for men in the hours-worked and employment samples (3,205,408 and 2,575,379 in the model (C) sterilisation subsample); 15,440,331 and 13,883,537 person-months excluding zero-hours months (2,839,834 and 2,441,788 in model (C)); 1,819,230 and 1,569,337 person-years for the income analyses (315,474 and 268,579 in model (C))

construction_notes: Monthly hours worked are aggregated across all jobs held in the relevant month, to capture total monthly hours
Hours of work are adjusted for observed days of parental leave, because for some employees with fixed contractual hours BFL hours are not adjusted during spells of parental leave
Child benefit payments are constructed precisely from population-register information on each family's number of children and the children's ages, and validated with the fourth-quarter register data

Monthly indicators equal to one if an individual has ever consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation (data from 1994 onwards); a family-level indicator equals one if either partner has consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation
The continuous treatment is the reduction in child benefits in thousand DKK in 2011 due to the reform, zero for the control group; 1000 DKK is approximately 160 USD
'Family's yearly benefits lost in 2011' is not exactly zero for the control group, because the treatment group is defined on the first two quarters of 2011 to avoid selection into treatment
All income measures are inverse-hyperbolic-sine transformed so that coefficients read as percentage changes and individuals with zero income can be included
98% winsorisation of all income measures: values below the 1st percentile are set to the 1st percentile and values above the 99th percentile to the 99th percentile
All measures of income are inflation-adjusted to 2014 levels
Child benefits are family-specific, so when constructing individual net-of-tax income including child benefits 50% is assigned to each parent
Parental age fixed effects and age-of-youngest-child fixed effects use each quarter of age, to control non-parametrically for age effects

m_t are 8 calendar month fixed effects accounting for within-quarter seasonality (not year*month), with the last calendar month of each quarter omitted to avoid collinearity with the year-quarter fixed effects

claims.statement: The paper tests whether the reduction in child benefits caused by the 2011 cap increased hours worked per month (including zero-hour months) of mothers, using a binary treatment indicator and model (A) controls.

treatment.label: 1.Intro x 1.Treat: being in the treatment group (family whose child benefits were cut by the 2011 cap) in the periods after the policy introduction

definition.value: W_i * Intro_t in Eqs. (2), (3) and (5). W_i = 1 if person i's family experienced a strictly positive reduction in child benefits due to the DKK 35,000 cap in the first two quarters of 2011; Intro_t = 1 in all periods after the policy introduction (payments from January 2011). Treatment group membership is fixed over time and therefore absorbed by the individual fixed effects, so only the interaction is included. Child benefits were computed from family composition in the population registers and validated against fourth-quarter payment data.

population.description: Mothers in married or cohabiting couples who in January 2011 had at least 2 children under 18 and no more than 4 children in total, at least 25 years old by September 2008 and under 60 by December 2014, present in the Danish population registers and in the sample throughout September 2008 to December 2014. Immigrants and children of immigrants, and parents of children receiving irregular child benefit payments, are excluded. Individuals self-employed at any point in the sample window are excluded, because hours worked are not observed for them.
population.ages: At least 25 years old by September 2008 and less than 60 years old by December 2014
population.period: September 2008 to December 2014 (monthly observations from October 2008)
subgroups_defined: Treatment group: families with a strictly positive reduction in child benefits due to the cap in Q1 and/or Q2 2011
Control group: families not affected by the cap in the first two quarters of 2011
population.selection: Balanced panel: individuals not present in the Danish population registers and in the sample for the entire period September 2008 to December 2014 are dropped. Treatment and control groups are fixed, defined by whether the family experienced a strictly positive reduction in child benefits in the first two quarters of 2011.

identification.source_of_variation: The DKK 35,000 cap on total family child benefits, announced in May 2010 and applied to payments from January 2011, repealed from 2012. It cut benefits only for families with more and younger children (three-child families with at least one child under 3 or at least two children under 7, and all families with four or more children), and was based solely on the number and age composition of children, not on family income or labour market status.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the cap, the outcome would have evolved in parallel for the treatment and control groups, conditional on individual, parental-age and time fixed effects (and, in models B and C, family controls).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raw quarterly trends for the treatment and control groups; the fully generalised difference-in-differences estimates of Eq. (1) for models (A), (B) and (C); and a joint test of the pre-period quarter indicators, which can reject neither that they are jointly zero nor that they are jointly equal, at the 5% level.

key_assumptions.assumption: No selection into or out of treatment and no anticipation through fertility: groups are defined on the benefit loss in the first two quarters of 2011, because children conceived before the May 2010 announcement could still be born until March 2011, and group membership is then fixed over time.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Timing argument about conception dates and the rule that a quarter's payment depends on the children present in the previous quarter.

implies_edges.from: Anticipation of the cap after the May 2010 announcement
implies_edges.to: Treatment group membership (benefit loss in Q1/Q2 2011)

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment assignment excludes income and labour market status: the cap depended only on the number and age composition of children and benefits were tax exempt, so the estimated labour supply effects are income effects alone, with no substitution effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional feature of the policy, stated in the introduction and in the hypotheses section.

implies_edges.from: Household earnings and labour market status
implies_edges.to: Exposure to the 2011 child benefit cap

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the control group is assumed not to respond to the cap. The authors note two-child families can be indirectly affected, because the marginal benefit of a third child fell, and address this with the sterilisation subsample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion of the small increase in hours and in participation for the control group, and Figure C.17 for the sterilisation subsample.

implies_edges.to: Control-group families' labour supply

key_assumptions.assumption: Model (A) conditions only on individual and parental-age fixed effects, so differing preferences for additional children - and hence fertility and parental-leave composition - remain an unobserved common cause. The authors concede part of the estimated effect is mechanical and read model (A) as an upper bound.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Placebo test in Appendix C.7, applying the empirical strategy at a point in time when families were not affected by the cap.

population.description: Mothers in married or cohabiting couples who in January 2011 had at least 2 children under 18 and no more than 4 children in total, at least 25 years old by September 2008 and under 60 by December 2014, present in the Danish population registers and in the sample throughout September 2008 to December 2014. Individuals self-employed at any point in the sample window are excluded, because hours worked are not observed for them. population.selection: Balanced panel: individuals not present in the Danish population registers and in the sample for the entire period September 2008 to December 2014 are dropped. identification.source_of_variation: The DKK 35,000 cap on total family child benefits, announced in May 2010 and applied to payments from January 2011, repealed from 2012. It cut benefits only for families with more and younger children (three-child families with at least one child under 3 or at least two children under 7, and all families with four or more children), and was based solely on the number and age composition of children, not on family income or labour market status.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the cap, the outcome would have evolved in parallel for the treatment and control groups, conditional on individual, parental-age and time fixed effects (and, in models B and C, family controls).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raw quarterly trends for the treatment and control groups; the fully generalised difference-in-differences estimates of Eq. (1) for models (A), (B) and (C); and a joint test of the pre-period quarter indicators, which can reject neither that they are jointly zero nor that they are jointly equal, at the 5% level.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the cap, the outcome would have evolved in parallel for the treatment and control groups, conditional on individual, parental-age and time fixed effects (and, in models B and C, family controls).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raw quarterly trends for the treatment and control groups; the fully generalised difference-in-differences estimates of Eq. (1) for models (A), (B) and (C); and a joint test of the pre-period quarter indicators, which can reject neither that they are jointly zero nor that they are jointly equal, at the 5% level.

key_assumptions.assumption: No selection into or out of treatment and no anticipation through fertility: groups are defined on the benefit loss in the first two quarters of 2011, because children conceived before the May 2010 announcement could still be born until March 2011, and group membership is then fixed over time.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Timing argument about conception dates and the rule that a quarter's payment depends on the children present in the previous quarter.

implies_edges.from: Anticipation of the cap after the May 2010 announcement
implies_edges.to: Treatment group membership (benefit loss in Q1/Q2 2011)

key_assumptions.assumption: Treatment assignment excludes income and labour market status: the cap depended only on the number and age composition of children and benefits were tax exempt, so the estimated labour supply effects are income effects alone, with no substitution effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional feature of the policy, stated in the introduction and in the hypotheses section.

implies_edges.from: Household earnings and labour market status
implies_edges.to: Exposure to the 2011 child benefit cap

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the control group is assumed not to respond to the cap. The authors note two-child families can be indirectly affected, because the marginal benefit of a third child fell, and address this with the sterilisation subsample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion of the small increase in hours and in participation for the control group, and Figure C.17 for the sterilisation subsample.

implies_edges.from: Exposure to the 2011 child benefit cap (treated families)
implies_edges.to: Control-group families' labour supply

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning on age-of-youngest-child and number-of-children fixed effects removes the fertility and parental-leave composition channel, leaving the income effect. The authors concede these controls may themselves be affected by the treatment (a bad control problem) and that the control group's own fertility response may bias model (B) downwards.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Comparison of models (A), (B) and (C); placebo test in Appendix C.7; the bad-control discussion citing Angrist and Pischke (2008).

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection on finalised fertility: restricting the sample to families where at least one parent consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation before the policy announcement, and excluding families with a child below age 3 throughout, fixes preferences for additional children across the groups and shuts down the fertility response.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sterilisation is a common procedure in Denmark after finalising fertility (Figure C.26); the two restrictions must be imposed together, since conditioning on sterilisation alone would compare different types of families.

implies_edges.from: Pre-announcement sterilisation consultation and no child under 3
implies_edges.to: Inclusion in the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Even with fertility preferences fixed, preferences for leisure and time with children may still differ between families with different numbers of children; the authors argue the estimate is then a lower bound for families with fewer children.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued, not tested. Four-child families are kept in the control group when at least one but no more than two children are over 18, and age of youngest child is controlled for.

population.description: Fathers in married or cohabiting couples who in January 2011 had at least 2 children under 18 and no more than 4 children in total, at least 25 years old by September 2008 and under 60 by December 2014, present in the Danish population registers and in the sample throughout September 2008 to December 2014. Immigrants and children of immigrants, and parents of children receiving irregular child benefit payments, are excluded. Individuals self-employed at any point in the sample window are excluded, because hours worked are not observed for them. The sample is further limited to families in which at least one parent consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation prior to the announcement of the policy, excluding families with young children (below the age of 3) throughout the sample period.

population.selection: Balanced panel: individuals not present in the Danish population registers and in the sample for the entire period September 2008 to December 2014 are dropped. Treatment and control groups are fixed, defined by whether the family experienced a strictly positive reduction in child benefits in the first two quarters of 2011. identification.source_of_variation: The DKK 35,000 cap on total family child benefits, announced in May 2010 and applied to payments from January 2011, repealed from 2012. It cut benefits only for families with more and younger children (three-child families with at least one child under 3 or at least two children under 7, and all families with four or more children), and was based solely on the number and age composition of children, not on family income or labour market status.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the cap, the outcome would have evolved in parallel for the treatment and control groups, conditional on individual, parental-age and time fixed effects (and, in models B and C, family controls).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raw quarterly trends for the treatment and control groups; the fully generalised difference-in-differences estimates of Eq. (1) for models (A), (B) and (C); and a joint test of the pre-period quarter indicators, which can reject neither that they are jointly zero nor that they are jointly equal, at the 5% level.

key_assumptions.assumption: No selection into or out of treatment and no anticipation through fertility: groups are defined on the benefit loss in the first two quarters of 2011, because children conceived before the May 2010 announcement could still be born until March 2011, and group membership is then fixed over time.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Timing argument about conception dates and the rule that a quarter's payment depends on the children present in the previous quarter.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional feature of the policy, stated in the introduction and in the hypotheses section.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the control group is assumed not to respond to the cap. The authors note two-child families can be indirectly affected, because the marginal benefit of a third child fell, and address this with the sterilisation subsample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion of the small increase in hours and in participation for the control group, and Figure C.17 for the sterilisation subsample.

implies_edges.from: Exposure to the 2011 child benefit cap (treated families)
implies_edges.to: Control-group families' labour supply

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning on age-of-youngest-child and number-of-children fixed effects removes the fertility and parental-leave composition channel, leaving the income effect. The authors concede these controls may themselves be affected by the treatment (a bad control problem) and that the control group's own fertility response may bias model (B) downwards.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Comparison of models (A), (B) and (C); placebo test in Appendix C.7; the bad-control discussion citing Angrist and Pischke (2008).

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection on finalised fertility: restricting the sample to families where at least one parent consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation before the policy announcement, and excluding families with a child below age 3 throughout, fixes preferences for additional children across the groups and shuts down the fertility response.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sterilisation is a common procedure in Denmark after finalising fertility (Figure C.26); the two restrictions must be imposed together, since conditioning on sterilisation alone would compare different types of families.

key_assumptions.assumption: Even with fertility preferences fixed, preferences for leisure and time with children may still differ between families with different numbers of children; the authors argue the estimate is then a lower bound for families with fewer children.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued, not tested. Four-child families are kept in the control group when at least one but no more than two children are over 18, and age of youngest child is controlled for.

population.selection: Balanced panel: individuals not present in the Danish population registers and in the sample for the entire period September 2008 to December 2014 are dropped. identification.source_of_variation: The DKK 35,000 cap on total family child benefits, announced in May 2010 and applied to payments from January 2011, repealed from 2012. It cut benefits only for families with more and younger children (three-child families with at least one child under 3 or at least two children under 7, and all families with four or more children), and was based solely on the number and age composition of children, not on family income or labour market status.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the cap, the outcome would have evolved in parallel for the treatment and control groups, conditional on individual, parental-age and time fixed effects (and, in models B and C, family controls).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raw quarterly trends for the treatment and control groups; the fully generalised difference-in-differences estimates of Eq. (1) for models (A), (B) and (C); and a joint test of the pre-period quarter indicators, which can reject neither that they are jointly zero nor that they are jointly equal, at the 5% level.

key_assumptions.assumption: No selection into or out of treatment and no anticipation through fertility: groups are defined on the benefit loss in the first two quarters of 2011, because children conceived before the May 2010 announcement could still be born until March 2011, and group membership is then fixed over time.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Timing argument about conception dates and the rule that a quarter's payment depends on the children present in the previous quarter.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional feature of the policy, stated in the introduction and in the hypotheses section.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the control group is assumed not to respond to the cap. The authors note two-child families can be indirectly affected, because the marginal benefit of a third child fell, and address this with the sterilisation subsample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion of the small increase in hours and in participation for the control group, and Figure C.17 for the sterilisation subsample.

implies_edges.from: Exposure to the 2011 child benefit cap (treated families)
implies_edges.to: Control-group families' labour supply

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning on age-of-youngest-child and number-of-children fixed effects removes the fertility and parental-leave composition channel, leaving the income effect. The authors concede these controls may themselves be affected by the treatment (a bad control problem) and that the control group's own fertility response may bias model (B) downwards.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Comparison of models (A), (B) and (C); placebo test in Appendix C.7; the bad-control discussion citing Angrist and Pischke (2008).

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection on finalised fertility: restricting the sample to families where at least one parent consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation before the policy announcement, and excluding families with a child below age 3 throughout, fixes preferences for additional children across the groups and shuts down the fertility response.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sterilisation is a common procedure in Denmark after finalising fertility (Figure C.26); the two restrictions must be imposed together, since conditioning on sterilisation alone would compare different types of families.

key_assumptions.assumption: Even with fertility preferences fixed, preferences for leisure and time with children may still differ between families with different numbers of children; the authors argue the estimate is then a lower bound for families with fewer children.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued, not tested. Four-child families are kept in the control group when at least one but no more than two children are over 18, and age of youngest child is controlled for.

identification.source_of_variation: The DKK 35,000 cap on total family child benefits, announced in May 2010 and applied to payments from January 2011, repealed from 2012. key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the cap, the outcome would have evolved in parallel for the treatment and control groups, conditional on individual, parental-age and time fixed effects (and, in models B and C, family controls).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raw quarterly trends for the treatment and control groups; the fully generalised difference-in-differences estimates of Eq. identification.source_of_variation: The DKK 35,000 cap on total family child benefits, announced in May 2010 and applied to payments from January 2011, repealed from 2012. key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the cap, the outcome would have evolved in parallel for the treatment and control groups, conditional on individual, parental-age and time fixed effects (and, in models B and C, family controls).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raw quarterly trends for the treatment and control groups; the fully generalised difference-in-differences estimates of Eq. key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the cap, the outcome would have evolved in parallel for the treatment and control groups, conditional on individual, parental-age and time fixed effects (and, in models B and C, family controls).

key_assumptions.supported_by: Sterilisation is a common procedure in Denmark after finalising fertility (Figure C.26); the two restrictions must be imposed together, since conditioning on sterilisation alone would compare different types of families.

population.selection: Balanced panel: individuals not present in the Danish population registers and in the sample for the entire period September 2008 to December 2014 are dropped. identification.source_of_variation: The DKK 35,000 cap on total family child benefits, announced in May 2010 and applied to payments from January 2011, repealed from 2012. It cut benefits only for families with more and younger children (three-child families with at least one child under 3 or at least two children under 7, and all families with four or more children), and was based solely on the number and age composition of children, not on family income or labour market status.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: absent the cap, the outcome would have evolved in parallel for the treatment and control groups, conditional on individual, parental-age and time fixed effects (and, in models B and C, family controls).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raw quarterly trends for the treatment and control groups; the fully generalised difference-in-differences estimates of Eq. (1) for models (A), (B) and (C); and a joint test of the pre-period quarter indicators, which can reject neither that they are jointly zero nor that they are jointly equal, at the 5% level.

key_assumptions.assumption: No selection into or out of treatment and no anticipation through fertility: groups are defined on the benefit loss in the first two quarters of 2011, because children conceived before the May 2010 announcement could still be born until March 2011, and group membership is then fixed over time.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Timing argument about conception dates and the rule that a quarter's payment depends on the children present in the previous quarter.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional feature of the policy, stated in the introduction and in the hypotheses section.

implies_edges.from: Household earnings and labour market status
implies_edges.to: Exposure to the 2011 child benefit cap

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: the control group is assumed not to respond to the cap. The authors note two-child families can be indirectly affected, because the marginal benefit of a third child fell, and address this with the sterilisation subsample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion of the small increase in hours and in participation for the control group, and Figure C.17 for the sterilisation subsample.

implies_edges.from: Exposure to the 2011 child benefit cap (treated families)
implies_edges.to: Control-group families' labour supply

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning on age-of-youngest-child and number-of-children fixed effects removes the fertility and parental-leave composition channel, leaving the income effect. The authors concede these controls may themselves be affected by the treatment (a bad control problem) and that the control group's own fertility response may bias model (B) downwards.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Comparison of models (A), (B) and (C); placebo test in Appendix C.7; the bad-control discussion citing Angrist and Pischke (2008).

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection on finalised fertility: restricting the sample to families where at least one parent consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation before the policy announcement, and excluding families with a child below age 3 throughout, fixes preferences for additional children across the groups and shuts down the fertility response.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sterilisation is a common procedure in Denmark after finalising fertility (Figure C.26); the two restrictions must be imposed together, since conditioning on sterilisation alone would compare different types of families.

key_assumptions.assumption: Even with fertility preferences fixed, preferences for leisure and time with children may still differ between families with different numbers of children; the authors argue the estimate is then a lower bound for families with fewer children.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued, not tested. Four-child families are kept in the control group when at least one but no more than two children are over 18, and age of youngest child is controlled for.
